title: Mariner Retail - Adaptive Burst POC: concurrency & cost sensitivity
content:
Executive summary:
This POC evaluated an adaptive-burst serving strategy for Mariner Retail's customer-facing product search and chat endpoints. Goal: demonstrate how a combination of dynamic concurrency targets, lightweight model fallbacks, and prefix caching affects latency tail (p95/p99), steady-state throughput, and per-token cost during traffic microbursts. Tests were run against a representative retail workload (mix of short queries, multi-turn chat, and long product descriptions) captured from Mariner's staging traces.

Top-level findings (short):
- Adaptive-burst with a two-tier model routing (primary 13B quantized + fallback 7B quantized) reduced p99 tail during 10x microbursts by ~40% while increasing steady-state token throughput by ~25% compared to single-model steady serving.
- Caching hot prefixes (customer search prefixes) provided the single biggest cost/latency benefit: cache hit rates of 22-28% yielded a 12-18% reduction in overall token bill and 30-45% reduction in p95 latencies for search queries.
- Aggressive int4 quantization on the primary model increased throughput 1.6x but caused a measurable drop in synthetic QA accuracy (EM down ~2.1%). Mariner may accept this trade for low-criticality recommendation responses but not for invoice/checkout dialogs.
- Cold-start cost for on-demand pools is non-trivial: first-request latency averaged 11–22s depending on instance type. Maintain a small warm pool for 99.9% availability of sub-second first-response.

Objectives and acceptance criteria:
- Demonstrate ability to handle 10x baseline QPS microbursts within 2x cost increase and with p99 <= 1.2s for chat endpoints.
- Show a viable rollout strategy for adaptive model routing with clear SLO fallbacks.
- Produce actionable configuration recommendations (batching, cache TTL, warm pool size, quantization profile).

Test matrix and methodology:
- Models tested: primary = retail-13b-open (4-bit quantized pipeline), fallback = retail-7b-lite (4-bit), and a high-quality reference 13b FP16 for diff checks.
- HW variants: H100-80GB (prod target), A100-40GB (cost-optimized), and a small gpus pool for dev (T4 equivalent).
- Traffic shape: baseline steady QPS 40 req/s for single-tenant Mariner workload; microburst scenarios of 4x and 10x with Poisson arrivals. Session lengths: short (avg 7 tokens req), medium (40 tokens), long (200 tokens). Multi-turn sessions simulated with cached KV injected.
- Duration: warmup 10m, steady-state 30m, burst window 5m, cool-down 10m per run. Metrics collected at 1s resolution.
- Harness: Redwood stress-harness v2 with histogramd aggregation + token accounting. Quality checks against a labelled eval set from Mariner (n=1,200 queries).

Key configuration knobs explored:
- Adaptive routing window (when to switch to fallback): thresholds tested 200ms, 400ms, 800ms observed p95 on primary.
- Batching target: dynamic continuous batching vs fixed-size (16/32/64).
- KV/prefix cache TTL: 30s, 2m, 10m.
- Warm pool sizes: 0, 2, 6 pre-warmed reps per region.
- Quantization profiles: none (FP16), int8, int4 (GPTQ-like) with activation clipping.

Results summary (representative numbers, H100 target environment):
- Steady-state (no burst):
  - Primary (13B int4) p50=38ms, p95=180ms, p99=330ms, throughput=1450 tok/s per replica, cost est = $8.4 per 1M tokens
  - Primary + fallback adaptive: p50=40ms, p95=175ms, p99=290ms, throughput effective=1800 tok/s, cost est = $9.6 per 1M tokens
- 10x burst window (Poisson) w/o adaptive routing:
  - p99 climbed to 1.9s, error rate (429s/timeouts) increased 2.9% at default timeouts, observed queueing and cold starts.
- 10x burst w/ adaptive routing + cache TTL 2m + warm pool=4:
  - p99 reduced to 1.1s, drop in client-observed errors to 0.4%, effective throughput improved by ~24% vs single-model baseline, token cost +14% vs baseline but 32% lower than naive scale-to-max replica approach.

Cost model notes (high level):
- Cost components: GPU instance-hour, network egress, memory persistence (KV cache), and cold-start overhead (extra short-lived replica spins).
- Example midpoint numbers: scaling naive to meet peak required 6x steady replicas -> cost 6x baseline. Adaptive routing required ~2.3x effective capacity (mixture of full replicas + cheap fallback instances) -> ~2.3x cost. Net savings vs naive peak autoscale = ~62%.
- Cache ROI: with 25% hot-prefix hit rate, ~15% net token savings across workload observed; TTL=2m hits sweet-spot between staleness and hit-rate.

Detailed observations and anomalies:
- Tail behavior driven by queueing under continuous batching: large batch sizes reduce avg token cost but amplify p99 during bursts. We found dynamic small-bound batching (upper bound 32 tokens, lower bound 8) gives best cost/latency tradeoff for Mariner's mixed query length distribution.
- Fallback model quality delta visible for complex multi-step queries (EM drop ~4% vs reference); route non-critical endpoints (search suggestions, quick reorder prompts) to fallback, keep FP16/ref for checkout flows.
- Cold start variance: H100 on new warm pool init takes ~10-12s to reach ready; model load pre-warming plus lazy mem-map cuts this to 4–6s. Consider snapshotting / fast-launch images for further improvement.
- Kernel selection changes (mixed attention kernels) on A100 produced intermittent higher p95; runtime should pin kernel selection per model/seq-length during runs to stabilize tail.

Suggested production configuration for Mariner (initial rollout):
1) Primary serving: retail-13b int4 on H100 with dynamic batching (8-32) + prefix cache TTL 120s.
2) Fallback: retail-7b-lite int4 on cheaper instances for burst absorb; enable automatic routing when queue latency > 250ms for >5s.
3) Warm pool: maintain 4 pre-warmed primary replicas per region; allow short-lived fallback spin-ups for spikes.
4) Telemetry: enable token-level cost, per-route p50/p95/p99, cache hit-rate dashboards, and automatic alerts when p99 > 900ms for 2m.
5) Rollout plan: 1-week canary (10% traffic) -> 30% with fallback policy -> 100% with rollback guard. Run qualitative evals on the labelled set after each step.

Risks and mitigations:
- Quality regressions from int4: assign critical intents to FP16 route and apply evaluation guards with auto-fallback to FP16 on detected hallucination patterns.
- Undersized warm pool causing transient errors: adopt conservative warm pool (4) while monitoring 99.9% availability windows.
- Unexpected kernel regressions on A100: pin kernel versions and run quick nightly tail-latency canaries.

Next steps / action items:
- SE & Infra: schedule a 2-week pilot implementing the above prod config in staging. (owner: Marco Diaz, ETA: 2027-01-10)
- Product: classify intents that can tolerate fallback routing (owner: Priya Shah, ETA: 2026-12-22)
- Eng: add an automated roll-forward test that verifies quality on the eval set after any quantization change (owner: Liam O'Connor, ETA: 2026-12-30)
- Ops: build a warm-pool autosizing probe that recommends warm pool size based on observed burst patterns (owner: Zara Ibrahim, ETA: 2027-01-07)

Appendix: sample metric snippets (H100 primary replica)
- 1-minute hist snapshot during 10x burst with adaptive routing: p50=82ms, p95=410ms, p99=1.11s, 12% 429/timeouts w/o warm pool -> 0.4% with warm pool.
- Cache hit distribution: top-1% prefixes = 58% of hits; tail of prefixes long (80% of prefixes have <3 hits/day).

Notes on reproducibility and artifacts:
- Full harness config and run scripts: https://github.com/redwood-inference/poc-mariner
- Raw traces and histograms uploaded to Confluence under the linked page. Re-runs should use the same random seed and the harness's pre-recorded session shapes for parity.

Concluding remark:
Adaptive burst with targeted fallback routing and conservative prefix caching gives Mariner Retail a practical path to retain low tail latency during unpredictable microbursts while avoiding full peak provisioning costs. There are trade-offs around quantization quality that need product-level intent gating; the recommended rollout balances cost and customer-facing quality for immediate wins.
